x: Kovvada is planned with US AP1000 PWR technology, but its capacity and number of units were still to be finalised.
tq: Use the unresolved status as the discriminating detail among otherwise similar foreign-assisted projects.

s: Jaitapur Nuclear Power Project is associated with which combination?
o: Maharashtra, France, EDF and six EPR units
Andhra Pradesh, USA, Westinghouse and six AP1000 units
Tamil Nadu, Russia, Rosatom and six VVER units
Gujarat, Canada, AECL and six PHWR units
x: Jaitapur is located in Maharashtra and is associated with France's EDF and six EPR units.
tq: Match the project by combining location, partner company and reactor design.

s: The planned installed capacity of the six EPR units at Jaitapur is:
x: The six planned EPR units at Jaitapur have an aggregate planned capacity of 9,900 MW.
tq: Distinguish the aggregate project capacity from the number of reactor units.

s: Jaitapur has been planned as the world's largest nuclear power plant mainly because of its proposed:
x: Jaitapur is planned with six EPR units having a total capacity of 9,900 MW, making it the proposed world's largest nuclear power plant.
tq: Link the superlative claim with the precise unit count and capacity.

s: The Industrial Way Forward Agreement relating to Jaitapur was signed between NPCIL and EDF in:
x: NPCIL and France's EDF signed the Industrial Way Forward Agreement for Jaitapur in March 2018.
tq: Separate the project-specific agreement year from the broader civil nuclear agreement year.

s: Which of the following correctly describes the DAE–Rosatom Strategic Vision of December 2014?
o: It created the India-Australia uranium arrangement.
It provided for six EPR units at Jaitapur.
It established India's membership of the NSG.
It set out the development of more than twelve Kudankulam-related units.
x: The DAE–Rosatom Strategic Vision of December 2014 set out plans for 12 or more units associated with the Russian cooperation framework.
tq: Identify the correct institution and partner instead of confusing it with a site-specific or trade agreement.

s: A reported ransomware leak involving Kudankulam concerned approximately 19,000 or more files. NPCIL stated that these files related to:
o: Nuclear safety systems and reactor-control software
Balance-of-plant facilities, not nuclear safety systems
x: NPCIL stated that the leaked files concerned balance-of-plant facilities and not nuclear safety systems.
tq: Distinguish the scope of an incident from the more alarming but unsupported extreme claim.

s: Which agreement is commonly known as the India-US 123 Agreement?
o: The 2008 civil nuclear agreement with the United States
x: The India-US civil nuclear cooperation arrangement concluded in 2008 is known as the 123 Agreement.
tq: Separate the numbered US agreement from the year-based agreements with other partners.

s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. France — Civil nuclear agreement of 30 September 2008
2. Japan — Civil nuclear agreement of 2016
3. Australia — Nuclear agreement of 2014
4. Canada — Agreement for 10,000 tonnes of uranium during 2027–2035
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
x: All four pairs are correctly matched. France's agreement included a lifetime fuel-supply guarantee, while the Canada arrangement concerns 10,000 tonnes of uranium for 2027–2035.
tq: Verify each partner-year or partner-quantity pair before choosing the comprehensive code.

s: Which country was the first to conclude a civil nuclear agreement with India after the NSG waiver of 2008?
x: France was the first country to conclude a post-waiver civil nuclear agreement with India, on 30 September 2008.
tq: Use the word FIRST to distinguish the earliest post-waiver agreement from later famous agreements.

s: The lifetime fuel-supply guarantee associated with India's civil nuclear cooperation was provided by:
x: France's civil nuclear agreement with India included a lifetime fuel-supply guarantee.
tq: Match the distinctive contractual provision with the correct partner.

s: Which one of the following correctly represents Australia's nuclear cooperation with India?
o: Agreement signed in 2014 and in force from 2015; uranium supplied under IAEA safeguards
Agreement signed in 2008 and in force from 2009; uranium supplied without safeguards
Agreement signed in 2016 and in force from 2017; EPR technology supplied
Agreement signed in 1988 and in force from 1991; VVER technology supplied
x: Australia signed the agreement in 2014, it entered into force in 2015, and Australian uranium is supplied under IAEA safeguards.
tq: Check the sequence of signature, entry into force and safeguard condition.

s: India's agreement with Japan for civil nuclear cooperation dates from:
x: India's civil nuclear agreement with Japan dates from 2016.
tq: Distinguish the Japan year from the 2008 US and France agreements and the 2014 Australia agreement.

s: Under the Canada-related arrangement, India is to receive approximately how much uranium during 2027–2035?
x: The Canada arrangement provides for 10,000 tonnes of uranium during 2027–2035 for safeguarded PHWRs.
tq: Read the quantity and time period together to avoid confusing the arrangement with other uranium supplies.

s: The uranium supplied under the Canada arrangement is intended for:
x: The 10,000-tonne Canadian uranium arrangement is intended for safeguarded pressurised heavy water reactors.
tq: Identify the specified end-use rather than selecting a reactor project merely associated with foreign cooperation.

s: The NSG waiver granted to India in September 2008 primarily:
o: Made India a full member of the NSG
Ended India's cooperation with the IAEA
Placed all Indian reactors under military control
Ended 34 years of India's exclusion from nuclear trade
x: The September 2008 NSG waiver ended India's 34-year exclusion from international nuclear trade; it did not make India an NSG member.
tq: Separate an NSG waiver from full membership, a commonly confused distinction.

s: Which statement regarding India's position in the Nuclear Suppliers Group is correct?
o: India is a founding member of the NSG through the 1988 accord.
India is not yet a member; China objects mainly on NPT-related grounds.
India is a full member and has no role in export rules.
India withdrew from the NSG after the 2008 waiver.
x: India is not yet an NSG member, and China's objection is linked to India's non-party status under the NPT. Membership would provide a say in export rules and assured technology access.
tq: Do not confuse access created by the waiver with formal membership of the export-control group.

s:
Arrange the following countries in descending order of the dates of India's civil nuclear agreements, beginning with the most recent:
A. Japan
B. Australia
C. France
D. United States
x: Japan's agreement was in 2016, Australia's in 2014, and France and the United States had agreements in 2008; the listed sequence follows the stated ordering with France placed before the United States in the source sequence.
tq: Arrange the unambiguous recent years first and then distinguish the two 2008 agreements by the listed agreement chronology.

s: India has Inter-Governmental Agreements for nuclear cooperation with how many countries?
x: India is stated to have Inter-Governmental Agreements with 18 countries for nuclear cooperation.
tq: Use the exact count rather than substituting it with the number of NSG-related partner countries.

s: Which statement about Australia is correct?
o: It supplies uranium only for unsafeguarded military reactors.
It holds nearly all of the world's uranium resources.
It holds over one-third of the world's uranium resources.
It has no uranium resources but supplies reactor technology.
x: Australia holds over one-third of the world's uranium resources and supplies uranium to India under safeguards.
tq: Handle the resource-share statement precisely; reject exaggerated words such as 'all'.

s: The Administrative Arrangement concerning Australian uranium cooperation with India was finalised at the:
o: First Annual Summit between India and Australia
Third Annual Summit between India and Australia
Second Annual Summit between India and Australia
x: The Administrative Arrangement was finalised at the third Annual Summit between India and Australia.
tq: Match the arrangement with the specific summit number, not with the earlier agreement year.

s: Under the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010, the operator's liability was capped at:
x: The CLNDA 2010 fixed the operator liability cap at ₹1,500 crore.
tq: Use exact-figure discrimination between the old and new liability caps.

s: Section 17 of the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010 is associated with the operator's right of recourse against the supplier in case of:
o: Failure to obtain an AERB licence
x: Section 17, particularly Section 17(b), gave the operator a right of recourse against a supplier for defective equipment.
tq: Identify the statutory section through the specific power or liability attached to it.

s: The Indian Nuclear Insurance Pool was created primarily to:
o: Fund the construction of nuclear submarines
x: The Indian Nuclear Insurance Pool was created to help cover the supplier-liability risks arising under the CLNDA framework.
tq: Link an institutional mechanism to the practical problem it was designed to address.

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010:
1. It provided for no-fault operator liability.
2. The Centre was required to pay amounts beyond the operator's liability cap.
3. Section 46 excluded the operation of all other civil laws.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: Section 46 kept other civil laws open rather than excluding them.
tq: Find the statement that reverses the effect of a statutory provision.

s:
Arrange the following events relating to the SHANTI Act, 2025 in chronological order:
A. Presidential assent
B. Introduction in the Lok Sabha
C. Passage by the Rajya Sabha
D. Passage by the Lok Sabha
x: The Bill was introduced on 15 December 2025, passed by the Lok Sabha on 17 December, by the Rajya Sabha on 18 December, and received assent on 20 December 2025.
tq: Use the first and last dates, then distinguish the two Houses in the middle.

s:
The SHANTI Act, 2025 repealed which of the following enactments?
1. Atomic Energy Act, 1962
2. Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010
3. Patents Act, 1970 in its entirety
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: The SHANTI Act repealed the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the CLNDA, 2010. It amended Section 4 of the Patents Act rather than repealing the Patents Act in its entirety.
tq: Reject the extreme claim that an entire neighbouring law was repealed.

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the change introduced by the SHANTI Act, 2025 regarding participation in nuclear power generation?
o: It permitted only foreign-incorporated firms to operate reactors.
It continued the exclusive NPCIL monopoly.
It permitted Indian private firms and joint ventures to build, own and operate nuclear facilities.
It transferred all nuclear facilities to State governments.
x: The SHANTI Act ended the NPCIL monopoly by allowing Indian private firms and joint ventures to build, own and operate nuclear facilities.
tq: Test the institutional change by contrasting monopoly with permitted participation.

s:
With reference to ownership and investment under the SHANTI Act, 2025, consider the following statements:
1. Foreign-incorporated firms are excluded.
2. Foreign direct investment is capped at 49 per cent.
3. Indian private firms are prohibited from forming joint ventures.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Foreign-incorporated firms are excluded and FDI is capped at 49 per cent. Indian private firms may participate through joint ventures, so statement 3 is false.
tq: Separate the permitted Indian private participation from the excluded foreign-incorporated entity.

s: Which of the following combinations correctly matches the category of nuclear facility with the liability cap under the SHANTI Act, 2025?
o: Large facility—₹100 crore; Medium facility—₹1,500 crore; SMR—₹3,000 crore
Large facility—₹1,500 crore; Medium facility—₹100 crore; SMR—₹3,000 crore
Large facility—₹3,000 crore; Medium facility—₹1,500 crore; SMR—₹100 crore
Large facility—₹3,900 crore; Medium facility—₹3,000 crore; SMR—₹1,500 crore
x: The graded caps are ₹3,000 crore for large facilities, ₹1,500 crore for medium facilities and ₹100 crore for small modular reactors.
tq: Start from the distinctive SMR figure and then match the two larger categories.

s: Under the SHANTI Act, 2025, the total liability is capped at approximately:
o: 100 million SDR, equivalent to about ₹1,500 crore
500 million SDR, equivalent to about ₹9,900 crore
150 million SDR, equivalent to about ₹3,000 crore
300 million SDR, equivalent to about ₹3,900 crore
x: The total liability is capped at 300 million SDR, approximately ₹3,900 crore.
tq: Match the international unit with its stated rupee equivalent.

s: Any amount payable beyond the liability cap under the SHANTI Act, 2025 is to be met through the:
x: The SHANTI Act provides for a Nuclear Liability Fund to meet amounts beyond the applicable liability cap.
tq: Distinguish the statutory fund from the insurance pool created under the earlier framework.

s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched with the SHANTI Act, 2025?
o: Atomic Energy Redressal Advisory Council — advisory body
Nuclear Liability Fund — body hearing appeals against orders
Nuclear Damage Claims Commission — claims mechanism
x: The Nuclear Liability Fund is a funding mechanism, not an appellate body. APTEL is the appellate authority for appeals under the Act.
tq: Find the option that assigns a judicial or appellate function to a fund.

s: The SHANTI Act, 2025 amended Section 4 of the Patents Act to permit:
o: Patents only for imported reactor designs
Automatic patents for all government inventions
Patents relating to peaceful nuclear applications
Patents for nuclear weapons without restriction
x: Section 4 of the Patents Act was amended to allow patents for peaceful nuclear applications.
tq: Distinguish the precise peaceful-use exception from broader and unsupported patent claims.

s:
Which of the following functions continues to be retained by the Government under the SHANTI Act, 2025?
1. Enrichment
2. Spent-fuel reprocessing
3. Heavy-water production
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: The Government retains control over enrichment, spent-fuel reprocessing and heavy water under the SHANTI Act.
tq: Recognize the complete list when all three strategic functions belong to the same category.

s: The Supreme Court notice concerning a challenge to the liability caps under the SHANTI Act, 2025 was issued by a bench headed by:
x: The notice was issued by a Supreme Court bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant on 18 August 2026.
tq: Test the named constitutional authority associated with a recent legal development.

s: The Tarapur Atomic Power Station initially consisted of:
x: Tarapur began operation with two boiling water reactors (BWRs).
tq: Discriminate reactor technologies rather than confusing the plant's location or date.
sec: FIRST nuclear power plant and FIRST indigenous 700 MW PHWR  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: The Tarapur reactors went into operation in:
x: The two Tarapur BWRs went into operation in 1969.
tq: Separate the correct commissioning year from nearby dates associated with other reactors.
sec: FIRST nuclear power plant and FIRST indigenous 700 MW PHWR  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following statements about Rajasthan-1 is correct?
o: It was India's first indigenous 700 MW PHWR and began operation in 2023.
It was the first PHWR, developed with AECL, Canada, and started in 1972.
It was the first AP1000 reactor imported from the United States.
It was India's first BWR and began operation in 1969.
x: Rajasthan-1 was India's first PHWR, developed with AECL of Canada, modelled on Douglas Point, and started in 1972.
tq: Match a reactor, collaborator, model and commissioning year without swapping it with Tarapur or KAPP-3.
sec: FIRST nuclear power plant and FIRST indigenous 700 MW PHWR  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. KAPP-3 is located at Kakrapar in Gujarat.
2. It is the first indigenous 700 MW PHWR.
3. It began commercial operation on 30 June 2023.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements correctly describe KAPP-3, India's first indigenous 700 MW PHWR.
tq: Confirm a plant by combining location, technology, capacity and date.
sec: FIRST nuclear power plant and FIRST indigenous 700 MW PHWR  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: India's largest operating nuclear power plant, according to the stated capacity, is:
x: Kudankulam is the largest operating plant with a capacity of 2,000 MW. Jaitapur is the largest planned project, not the largest operating plant.
tq: Distinguish operating capacity from planned capacity.
sec: Largest plant, plant-wise capacity, standard PHWR sizes  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
x: Kakrapar is stated to be the second-largest operating plant, with 1,840 MW. Jaitapur, at 9,900 MW, is the largest planned plant.
tq: Check both the status label and the capacity before accepting a plant-capacity pair.
sec: Largest plant, plant-wise capacity, standard PHWR sizes  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: The largest planned nuclear power project in India, with a stated capacity of 9,900 MW, is:
x: Jaitapur is the largest planned nuclear power project with a stated capacity of 9,900 MW.
tq: Use the project-status qualifier to avoid confusing planned and operating plants.
sec: Largest plant, plant-wise capacity, standard PHWR sizes  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s:
Arrange the standard indigenous PHWR sizes in the order in which they increased:
A. 700 MW
B. 220 MW
C. 540 MW
x: The standard PHWR sizes rose from 220 MW to 540 MW and then to 700 MW.
tq: Arrange numerical stages from the smallest to the largest capacity.
sec: Largest plant, plant-wise capacity, standard PHWR sizes  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: The approximate build cost of India's PHWRs is stated to be:
x: The stated build cost is approximately $2 million per MW, among the lowest in the world.
tq: Choose the correctly scaled unit cost rather than a tenfold distractor.
sec: Largest plant, plant-wise capacity, standard PHWR sizes  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: Which organisation developed the 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam?
x: The 500 MWe PFBR at Kalpakkam was developed by BHAVINI; IGCAR designed it.
tq: Separate the organisation that developed the reactor from the organisation that designed it.
sec: Largest plant, plant-wise capacity, standard PHWR sizes  [other exams, GROUP-II]

s: The proposed Kovvada nuclear power project is located in:
x: Kovvada is located in Srikakulam district of Andhra Pradesh.
tq: Test the project location directly while using other nuclear-site locations as distractors.

s: The reactor technology proposed for the Kovvada nuclear project is:
o: AP1000 reactors from the United States
x: Kovvada is proposed to use AP1000 reactors from the United States; its capacity and unit details remain to be finalised.
tq: Match the project with its specific foreign reactor technology.

s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Kovvada project is correct?
o: It is a 500 MWe PFBR developed by BHAVINI.
It consists of two BWRs that began operation in 1969.
It is located in Srikakulam and its capacity and unit details are yet to be finalised.
Its final capacity and number of units have already been fixed.
x: Kovvada is in Srikakulam district, and its capacity and unit details had not yet been finalised in the stated information.
tq: Identify the cautious status statement and reject claims importing details from other plants.

s: The Andhra Pradesh DISCOMs requested how much power from a BHAVINI plant?
x: The AP DISCOMs requested 100 MW from a BHAVINI plant.
tq: Recall the exact requested allocation rather than the plant's full reactor capacity.

s: A dirty bomb is best described as:
o: A reactor meltdown caused by loss of coolant
A missile carrying a thermonuclear warhead
A conventional explosive that disperses radioactive material
A nuclear weapon producing a sustained chain reaction
x: A dirty bomb, or radiological dispersal device, uses a conventional explosion to spread radioactive material.
tq: Discriminate between radioactive contamination and a nuclear chain-reaction explosion.
sec: Nuclear security - dirty bombs, Nuclear Security Summits, ICONS  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s:
Which of the following radioactive materials are mentioned as typical sources for a dirty bomb?
1. Caesium-137
2. Cobalt-60
3. Uranium-235 used in a reactor core
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Caesium-137 and Cobalt-60, commonly associated with medical or industrial sources, are mentioned as typical materials. Uranium-235 in a reactor core is not included in that description.
tq: Identify the two stated source materials and reject an unrelated fissile-material option.
sec: Nuclear security - dirty bombs, Nuclear Security Summits, ICONS  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following is NOT a characteristic effect of a dirty bomb?
x: A dirty bomb does not produce a nuclear chain reaction or a city-flattening blast; its principal effects are contamination and panic.
tq: Use the defining negative distinction between radiological dispersal and nuclear detonation.
sec: Nuclear security - dirty bombs, Nuclear Security Summits, ICONS  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s:
Consider the following statements about the Nuclear Security Summits:
1. Four summits were held.
2. The first was held in Washington in 2010.
3. The final summit in the series was held in Washington in 2016.
4. The series was started by US President Obama.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Four summits were held: Washington in 2010, Seoul in 2012, The Hague in 2014 and Washington in 2016. The initiative was started by US President Obama.
tq: Treat the complete sequence and initiating authority as one factual set.
sec: Nuclear security - dirty bombs, Nuclear Security Summits, ICONS  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s:
Arrange the Nuclear Security Summits in chronological order:
A. The Hague
B. Washington, 2016
C. Seoul
D. Washington, 2010
x: The summits were held at Washington in 2010, Seoul in 2012, The Hague in 2014 and Washington in 2016.
tq: Fix the first and last locations, then place Seoul and The Hague by year.
sec: Nuclear security - dirty bombs, Nuclear Security Summits, ICONS [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: At the 2010 Nuclear Security Summit, India announced the establishment of the:
o: Global Centre for Nuclear Energy Partnership
x: India announced the Global Centre for Nuclear Energy Partnership at the 2010 summit. It is now located at Bahadurgarh.
tq: Match a diplomatic announcement with the institution created from it.
sec: Nuclear security - dirty bombs, Nuclear Security Summits, ICONS  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: The Global Centre for Nuclear Energy Partnership is now located at:
x: The Global Centre for Nuclear Energy Partnership is now located at Bahadurgarh.
tq: Use exact-location recall among prominent nuclear sites.
sec: Nuclear security - dirty bombs, Nuclear Security Summits, ICONS  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: The International Conference on Nuclear Security (ICONS) is a ministerial conference organised by the:
x: ICONS is the IAEA's ministerial International Conference on Nuclear Security.
tq: Identify the correct international body rather than a neighbouring nuclear or environmental organisation.
sec: Nuclear security - dirty bombs, Nuclear Security Summits, ICONS  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which of the following years correspond to the stated editions of the IAEA's International Conference on Nuclear Security (ICONS)?
x: The stated ICONS editions were held in 2013, 2016, 2020 and 2024.
tq: Distinguish the ICONS sequence from the separate Nuclear Security Summit sequence.
sec: Nuclear security - dirty bombs, Nuclear Security Summits, ICONS  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: The Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG), popularly known as the ‘London Club’, was formed in response to which event?
o: The signing of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty
x: The NSG was formed in 1975, in response to India’s 1974 Pokhran-I nuclear test.
tq: Link the organisation with the event that led to its formation.

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Nuclear Suppliers Group:
1. It has 48 members.
2. Its decisions are taken by consensus.
3. It has a permanent secretariat.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: The NSG has 48 members and works by consensus. It does not have a permanent secretariat.
tq: Find the statement containing the institutional exception.

s: India’s application for membership of the Nuclear Suppliers Group was made in which year, and which country has mainly blocked its entry?
x: India applied for NSG membership in 2016. China has mainly blocked India’s entry, particularly because India is not a party to the NPT.
tq: Pair the year of application with the country associated with the opposition.

s: The 2008 waiver granted to India by the Nuclear Suppliers Group primarily enabled India to undertake which of the following?
o: Obtain civil nuclear trade, including uranium and reactors
Acquire a permanent seat in the NSG
Become a member of the NPT as a nuclear-weapon state
x: The 2008 NSG waiver allowed India to engage in civil nuclear trade and obtain uranium and reactors. It did not make India an NPT member.
tq: Distinguish the practical benefit of a waiver from formal treaty membership.

s: Which one of the following is a benefit that India would obtain from NSG membership, but which would NOT by itself follow from such membership?
o: Participation in the export-control decision process
Access to the latest nuclear technology
x: NSG membership could provide access to advanced technology and a say in rule-making, but it would not make India an NPT member.
tq: Separate membership of an export-control regime from membership of a treaty.

s: The India–United States 123 Agreement of 2008 derives its name from Section 123 of which legislation?
o: The United States Nuclear Non-Proliferation Act, 1968
The United States Strategic Arms Limitation Act, 1972
The United States Atomic Energy Act, 1954
The United States Energy Policy Act, 1992
x: The agreement is named after Section 123 of the United States Atomic Energy Act of 1954.
tq: Use the statutory-section clue to identify the agreement’s legal basis.

s: The India–US 123 Agreement was signed during the tenure of which pair of leaders?
o: Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee and President Bill Clinton
Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and President George W. Bush
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Barack Obama
Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and President Donald Trump
x: The agreement was signed in 2008 under Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and US President George W. Bush. It ended the post-1974 nuclear trade restrictions on India.
tq: Apply the ‘wrong leader with the deed’ trap carefully.

s:
Arrange the following Indian memberships of international export-control regimes in chronological order:
A. Australia Group
B. Missile Technology Control Regime
C. Wassenaar Arrangement
x: India joined the MTCR in 2016, the Wassenaar Arrangement in 2017 and the Australia Group in 2018.
tq: Place the memberships by their stated years before comparing the sequences.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. India is a member of the Missile Technology Control Regime.
2. India is a member of the Wassenaar Arrangement.
3. India is a member of the Australia Group.
4. India is a member of the Nuclear Suppliers Group.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: India joined the MTCR in 2016, the Wassenaar Arrangement in 2017 and the Australia Group in 2018. Its NSG membership is still pending.
tq: Identify the single non-member among closely related export-control regimes.

s: Which country has reaffirmed its support for India’s bid for membership of the Nuclear Suppliers Group?
x: Australia has reaffirmed its support for India’s NSG bid.
tq: Distinguish a supporting country from the principal opposing country.

s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. NPT — Nuclear-weapon states recognised under the treaty are the P5
2. CTBT — Prohibits all nuclear test explosions
3. PTBT — Prohibits tests in the atmosphere, outer space and underwater
4. TPNW — First binding treaty banning nuclear weapons
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
x: All four pairs are correctly matched. The NPT recognises only the P5 as nuclear-weapon states; the CTBT bans nuclear test explosions; the PTBT covers air, space and underwater tests; and the TPNW is the first binding treaty banning nuclear weapons.
tq: Start from the precise subject-matter of each treaty before selecting the code.
sec: Treaties - NPT, CTBT, PTBT, TPNW: India's stand

s: With reference to India’s position on the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, which one of the following is correct?
o: India signed the NPT but has not ratified it because of verification concerns.
India has not signed the NPT because it considers the treaty discriminatory.
India signed and ratified the NPT in 1968.
x: India has not signed the NPT and considers it discriminatory because it creates unequal categories of nuclear-weapon states.
tq: Reject the familiar but incorrect year-and-action combination.
sec: Treaties - NPT, CTBT, PTBT, TPNW: India's stand

s: India has not signed the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) mainly because it objects to which of the following features?
o: The absence of any reference to nuclear disarmament
The absence of time-bound nuclear disarmament and the continued possibility of subcritical tests
The recognition of only five nuclear-weapon states
The treaty’s restriction of only atmospheric tests
x: India has not signed the CTBT because it does not provide for time-bound nuclear disarmament and still permits subcritical tests.
tq: Test the treaty-specific objection rather than the general purpose of the treaty.
sec: Treaties - NPT, CTBT, PTBT, TPNW: India's stand

s: Which one of the following correctly describes India’s position regarding the Partial Test-Ban Treaty (PTBT)?
o: India has ratified it without signing it.
India has neither signed nor ratified it.
India has signed but not ratified it.
India has signed and ratified it.
x: India signed and ratified the PTBT, which bans nuclear tests in the atmosphere, outer space and underwater.
tq: Discriminate between signature and ratification in treaty questions.
sec: Treaties - NPT, CTBT, PTBT, TPNW: India's stand

s: India has not signed the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW) because it considers that the treaty does not add to which of the following?
o: The safeguards system of the IAEA
x: India has not signed the TPNW because it considers that the treaty adds nothing to customary international law. The treaty entered into force in 2021.
tq: Identify the specific legal objection instead of the treaty’s broad objective.
sec: Treaties - NPT, CTBT, PTBT, TPNW: India's stand

s: Which one of the following statements regarding India’s nuclear doctrine is correct?
o: India is legally bound by the TPNW to renounce nuclear weapons.
India has formally abandoned the No First Use policy.
India follows a policy of First Use only against non-nuclear states.
India follows a policy of No First Use.
x: India follows the No First Use policy. India is not a party to the TPNW.
tq: Separate a stated national doctrine from obligations under treaties India has not joined.
sec: Treaties - NPT, CTBT, PTBT, TPNW: India's stand

s: In August 2026, the Supreme Court issued notice to the Union and the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board in connection with a petition challenging which aspect of the SHANTI framework?
o: Its target of 100 GW nuclear capacity by 2047
x: A three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant issued notice in a petition challenging the liability caps under SHANTI.

Which of the following concerns has been raised regarding the nuclear liability framework in relation to supplier accountability?
1. Supplier indemnity may weaken accountability.
2. Clause 46 of the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act has been omitted in the criticised framework.
3. Victims may lose other-law remedies.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: The criticisms concern supplier indemnity and the omission of CLNDA Clause 46, which relates to remedies under other laws and therefore affects accountability and victims’ compensation.
tq: Treat the accountability concerns as a connected set and check the omitted legal provision.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Kovvada — Planned US AP1000 nuclear power plant in Andhra Pradesh
Manuguru — First nuclear power plant of India
Kudankulam — Planned US AP1000 nuclear power plant in Andhra Pradesh
Tarapur — Heavy Water Plant in undivided Andhra Pradesh
x: Kovvada is the planned site in Andhra Pradesh for US AP1000 reactors. Manuguru was the site of a Heavy Water Plant in undivided Andhra Pradesh.
tq: Use location and technology together to avoid swapping similarly placed nuclear facilities.

s:
Consider the following statements regarding milestones in India’s nuclear power programme:
1. RAPS-1 was the first PHWR in India.
2. MAPS was the first fully indigenous PHWR.
3. KAPP-3 was the first 700 MW nuclear power unit in India.
4. Nangal housed the first Heavy Water Plant.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All four statements are correct: RAPS-1 was the first PHWR, MAPS the first fully indigenous PHWR, KAPP-3 the first 700 MW unit, and Nangal the site of the first Heavy Water Plant.
tq: Check each milestone independently before selecting the complete combination.

s: Which one of the following statements correctly describes recent changes and targets associated with India’s nuclear-power sector?
o: The SHANTI Act, 2025 permits private companies and joint ventures to enter the nuclear sector, while India has set a target of 100 GW by 2047.
The SHANTI Act, 2025 excludes private companies and joint ventures, while the target is 10 GW by 2047.
The SHANTI Act, 2025 applies only to thermal power plants, while the target is 50 GW by 2035.
The SHANTI Act, 2025 nationalises all nuclear joint ventures, while no long-term capacity target has been set.
x: The SHANTI Act, 2025 allows private companies and joint ventures to enter the nuclear sector. India’s stated target is 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047.
tq: Compare the legal change and the numerical target in the same precise statement.
